entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 2 Zep 2:1-15 . Exhortation to Repent before the Chaldean Invaders Come. Doom of Judah's Foes, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, with Their Idols, and Ethiopia and Assyria. 1. Gather yourselves-- to a religious assembly, to avert the judgment by prayers ( Joe 2:16 ) [Grotius]. Or, so as not to be dissipated "as chaff" ( Zep 2:2 ). The Hebrew is akin to a root meaning "chaff." Self-confidence and corrupt desires are the dissipation from which they are exhorted to gather themselves [Calvin]. The foe otherwise, like the wind, will scatter you "as the chaff." Repentance is the gathering of themselves meant. nation not desired-- (Compare 2Ch 21:20 ), that is, not desirable; unworthy of the grace or favor of God; and yet God so magnifies that grace as to be still solicitous for their safety, though they had destroyed themselves and forfeited all claims on His grace [Calvin]. The Margin from Chaldee Version has, "not desirous," namely of returning to God. Maurer and Gesenius translate, "Not waxing pale," that is, dead to shame. English Version is best.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12941"/><div sID="gen24223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12941"/><hi type="bold">2. Before the decree bring forth--</hi>that is, Before God's decree against you announced by me (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.1-Zeph.1.18">Zep 1:1-18</reference>) have its fulfilment. As the embryo lies hid in the womb, and then emerges to light in its own due time, so though God for a time hides His vengeance, yet He brings it forth at the proper season.<div eID="gen24223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the day pass as the chaff--</hi>that is, before the day for repentance pass, and with it you, the ungodly, pass away as the chaff (<reference osisRef="Job.21.18">Job 21:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.1.4">Psa 1:4</reference>). Maurer puts it parenthetically, "the day (that is, time) passes as the chaff (that is, most quickly)." Calvin, "before the decree bring forth" (the predicted vengeance), (then) the chaff (the Jews) shall pass in a day, that is, in a moment, though they thought that it would be long before they could be overthrown. English Version is best; the latter clause being explanatory of the former, and so the before being understood, not expressed. <div eID="gen24224" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12942"/><div sID="gen24225" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12942"/>3. As in <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1">Zep 2:1</reference> (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.12">Zep 1:12</reference>) he had warned the hardened among the people to humble themselves, so now he admonishes "the meek" to proceed in their right course, that so they may escape the general calamity (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.9">Psa 76:9</reference>). The meek bow themselves under God's chastisements to God's will, whereas the ungodly become only the more hardened by them.<div eID="gen24225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Seek ye the Lord--</hi>in contrast to those that "sought not the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.6">Zep 1:6</reference>). The meek are not to regard what the multitudes do, but seek God at once.<div eID="gen24226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his judgment--</hi>that is, law. The true way of "seeking the Lord" is to "work judgment," not merely to be zealous about outward ordinances.<div eID="gen24227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek meekness--</hi>not perversely murmuring against God's dealings, but patiently submitting to them, and composedly waiting for deliverance.<div eID="gen24228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it may be ye shall be hid--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.6">Am 5:6</reference>). This phrase does not imply doubt of the deliverance of the godly, but expresses the difficulty of it, as well that the ungodly may see the certainty of their doom, as also that the faithful may value the more the grace of God in their case (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17-1Pet.4.19">1Pe 4:17-19</reference>) [Calvin]. Compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.12">2Ki 25:12</reference>. <div eID="gen24229" type="x-p"/>

Compare 2Ki 25:12 .

So the Hebrew of the next clause, Ekron teeakeer. at the noonday-- when on account of the heat Orientals usually sleep, and military operations are suspended ( 2Sa 4:5 ). Hence an attack at noon implies one sudden and unexpected ( Jr 6:4 , 5 ; 15:8 ). Ekron-- Four cities of the Philistines are mentioned, whereas five was the normal number of their leading cities. Gath is omitted, being at this time under the Jews' dominion. David had subjugated it ( 1Ch 18:1 ). Under Joram the Philistines almost regained it ( 2Ch 21:16 ), but Uzziah ( 2Ch 26:6 ) and Hezekiah ( 2Ki 18:8 ) having conquered them, it remained under the Jews. Am 1:6 ; Zec 9:5 , 6 ; Jr 25:20 , similarly mention only four cities of the Philistines.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12945"/><div sID="gen24237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12945"/><hi type="bold">6. dwellings and cottages for shepherds--</hi>rather, "dwellings with cisterns" (that is, water-tanks dug in the earth) for shepherds. Instead of a thick population and tillage, the region shall become a pasturage for nomad shepherds' flocks. The Hebrew for "dug cisterns," Ceroth, seems a play on sounds, alluding to their name Cherethites (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.5">Zep 2:5</reference>): Their land shall become what their national name implies, a land of cisterns. Maurer translates, "Feasts for shepherds' (flocks)," that is, one wide pasturage. <div eID="gen24237" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12952"/><div sID="gen24254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12952"/>13. Here he passes suddenly to the north. Nineveh was destroyed by Cyaxares and Nabopolassar, 625 B.C. The Scythian hordes, by an inroad into Media and thence in the southwest of Asia (thought by many to be the forces described by Zephaniah, as the invaders of Judea, rather than the Chaldeans), for a while interrupted Cyaxares' operations; but he finally succeeded. Arbaces and Belesis previously subverted the Assyrian empire under Sardanapalus (that is, Pul?), 877 B.C. <div eID="gen24254" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 14. flocks-- of sheep; answering to "beasts" in the parallel clause. Wide pastures for sheep and haunts for wild beasts shall be where once there was a teeming population (compare Zep 2:6 ). Maurer, needlessly for the parallelism, makes it "flocks of savage animals." beasts of the nations-- that is, beasts of the earth ( Ge 1:24 ). Not as Rosenmuller, "all kinds of beasts that form a nation," that is, gregarious beasts ( Pr 30:25 , 26 ). cormorant-- rather, the "pelican" (so Psa 102:6 ; Is 34:11 , Margin). bittern-- ( Is 14:23 ). Maurer translates, "the hedgehog"; Henderson, "the porcupine." upper lintels-- rather, "the capitals of her columns," namely, in her temples and palaces [Maurer]. Or, "on the pomegranate-like knops at the tops of the houses" [Grotius]. their voice shall sing in the windows-- The desert-frequenting birds' "voice in the windows" implies desolation reigning in the upper parts of the palaces, answering to "desolation ... in the thresholds," that is, in the lower. he shall uncover the cedar work-- laying the cedar wainscoting on the walls, and beams of the ceiling, bare to wind and rain, the roof being torn off, and the windows and doors broken through. All this is designed as a consolation to the Jews that they may bear their calamities patiently, knowing that God will avenge them.

Nothing then seemed more improbable than that the capital of so vast an empire, a city sixty miles in compass, with walls one hundred feet high, and so thick that three chariots could go abreast on them, and with fifteen hundred towers, should be so totally destroyed that its site is with difficulty discovered. Yet so it is, as the prophet foretold.<div eID="gen24262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there is none beside me--</hi>This peculiar phrase, expressing self-gratulation as if peerless, is plainly adopted from <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">Is 47:8</reference>. The later prophets, when the spirit of prophecy was on the verge of departing, leaned more on the predictions of their predecessors.<div eID="gen24263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hiss--</hi>in astonishment at a desolation so great and sudden (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.8">1Ki 9:8</reference>); also in derision (<reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job 27:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">La 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.36">Eze 27:36</reference>). <chapter eID="Zeph.2"/>
entries.content_plain: 15. Nothing then seemed more improbable than that the capital of so vast an empire, a city sixty miles in compass, with walls one hundred feet high, and so thick that three chariots could go abreast on them, and with fifteen hundred towers, should be so totally destroyed that its site is with difficulty discovered. Yet so it is, as the prophet foretold. there is none beside me-- This peculiar phrase, expressing self-gratulation as if peerless, is plainly adopted from Is 47:8 . The later prophets, when the spirit of prophecy was on the verge of departing, leaned more on the predictions of their predecessors. hiss-- in astonishment at a desolation so great and sudden ( 1Ki 9:8 ); also in derision ( Job 27:23 ; La 2:15 ; Eze 27:36 ).
